background_notes.fact: For a smooth map v from an open subset of ℝ^n×ℝ to ℝ^m, the derivative in any available time or spatial coordinate s satisfies ∂_s(v·v)=2v·∂_s v. If v·v=1 in a neighborhood, this derivative is zero there.

background_notes.justification: Expand v·v as the finite sum of squared real components. The scalar product rule follows by writing the product difference quotient as the sum of two factors' difference quotients, using differentiability and hence continuity. Apply it to each component square and add the finite sum. A locally constant scalar function has zero difference quotients. Thus the calculation used to obtain F001 is valid.

background_notes.fact: For a C² Euclidean-valued map v near a point and a time or spatial coordinate s, ∂_s²(v·v)=2|∂_s v|²+2v·∂_s²v. Consequently a locally unit-length v satisfies v·∂_s²v=−|∂_s v|².

background_notes.justification: Differentiate the finite-component identity ∂_s(v·v)=2Σ_k v_k∂_s v_k once more. The scalar product rule gives 2Σ_k[(∂_s v_k)²+v_k∂_s²v_k]. This is the asserted formula by the Euclidean norm definition. For v·v=1 its second derivative is zero; dividing the identity by 2 gives the stated consequence. It applies separately to time and each spatial coordinate, without requiring mixed-derivative commutation.
